questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x-4,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{⏟}}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{⏟}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+2y=t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{t}+B{e}^{2t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta $ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0-3\alpha +2(\alpha t+\beta )=t-4
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
2\alpha t+(-3\alpha +2\beta )=t-4.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ -3\alpha +2\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\alpha =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\beta =-\frac{5}{4},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{2}t-\frac{5}{4}=\frac{2t-5}{4}.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5}{4}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Particular Solution For a Cauchy-Euler Equation Using Variation of Parameters
questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-3t{y}^{′}+3y=2{t}^{4}{e}^{t},\,t>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(t)=At+B{t}^{3}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ to this equation.

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\int {t}^{2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t=({t}^{2}-2t+2){e}^{t}+C
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the differential equation to the form

$$
{y}^{″}+P(t){y}^{′}+Q(t)y=f(t).
$$

So, we divide both sides of the given equation by ${t}^{2}.$ We get

$$
{y}^{″}-\frac{3}{t}{y}^{′}+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}}y=2{t}^{2}{e}^{t}.
$$

We notice that the forcing term $f(t)=2{t}^{2}{e}^{t}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions:

$$
{y}_{1}(t)=t,\,{y}_{2}(t)={t}^{3}
$$

First, let's compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =(t)({t}^{3})^{′}-{(t)}^{′}({t}^{3}) \\  & =3{t}^{3}-{t}^{3} \\  & =2{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(t)$ and ${y}_{2}(t)$ are independent.

According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution of the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(t) & ={y}_{1}(t)u(t)+{y}_{2}(t)v(t),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =-\int \frac{f(t){y}_{2}(t)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}t=-\int {t}^{2}{e}^{t}=-({t}^{2}-2t+2){e}^{t}, \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{f(t){y}_{1}(t)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(t) & ={y}_{1}(t)u(t)+{y}_{2}(t)v(t) \\  & =-t({t}^{2}-2t+2){e}^{t}+{t}^{3}{e}^{t} \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-2t){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation With Forcing
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-12y=4{x}^{2},\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-12y=0.
$$

Let $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-12] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -12 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-3$ and $\lambda =4.$
Therefore, the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{4}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{3}}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is proportional to ${x}^{2}.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}
$$

where $\alpha $ is the constant that is to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation and group the terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(2\alpha )-12(\alpha {x}^{2}) & =4{x}^{2} \\ (2\alpha -12\alpha ){x}^{2} & =4{x}^{2} \\ -10\alpha {x}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get $\alpha =-\frac{2}{5}.$

Hence, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{5}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & ={c}_{1}{x}^{4}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Particular Solution For a Cauchy-Euler Equation Using Variation of Parameters
questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}-4y={x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,x>0
$$

has the complimentary function ${y}_{c}(x)=\frac{A}{{x}^{2}}+B{x}^{2}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation. 

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:* 

$$
\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=4x({x}^{2}-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+({x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}+24)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the differential equation to the form

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=f(x).
$$

So, we divide both sides of the given equation by ${x}^{2}.$ We get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{x}{y}^{′}-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}y=x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We notice that the forcing term $f(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions:

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,{y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}
$$

First, let's compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}({x}^{2})^{′}-{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}^{′}{x}^{2} \\  & =2x(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-(-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}){x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2}{x} \\  & =\frac{4}{x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

According to the method of variation of parameters, the particular solution of the differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={y}_{1}(x)u(x)+{y}_{2}(x)v(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}\int {x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}(4x({x}^{2}-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+({x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}+24)\operatorname{sin}⁡x), \\ v(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={y}_{1}(x)u(x)+{y}_{2}(x)v(x) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})(-\frac{1}{4}(4x({x}^{2}-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+({x}^{4}-12{x}^{2}+24)\operatorname{sin}⁡x))+({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =(-x+\frac{6}{x})\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+3-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =(\frac{6}{x}-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(3-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ of the equation 

$$
{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-10y=5\operatorname{ln}⁡x,\,x>0.
$$

*Hint: Consider using the substitution $x={e}^{t}.$*

This Cauchy-Euler equation has non-polynomial forcing, but we are not given two fundamental solutions, so we cannot use variation of parameters.

However, if we make a substitution $x={e}^{t},$ we can transform the Cauchy-Euler equation into a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

Letting $x={e}^{t},$ we note that

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{t}=x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Then, we use the chain rule to compute the first and second derivatives. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & ={{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}_{⏟}}_{\text{product rule}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}}_{⏟}}_{\text{chain rule}}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-10y=5t.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is a second-order inhomogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients and polynomial forcing. 

Using the usual methods for solving second-order ODEs, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(t)=\frac{A}{{e}^{5t}}+B{e}^{2t}.
$$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}t}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{t}^{2}}=0.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation for $y(t):$

$$
0+3\alpha -10(\alpha t+\beta )=5t
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-10\alpha t-10\beta +3\alpha =t.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-10\alpha =5\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of }t) \\ -10\beta +3\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the constants}).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2}$ and $\beta =-\frac{3}{20},$ and so the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{t}{2}-\frac{3}{20}.
$$

Now, returning to the variable $x,$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{2}-\frac{3}{20}.
$$
